title: Toyota Crown Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Own
summary: Our definitive Toyota Crown buying guide covers the history and specs of the single model generation available, how much you can expect to pay for one, and which are the best and worst versions to buy.
body_markdown:
One of Toyota's longest-running nameplates, the Crown returned to the U.S. after a five-decade absence. The modern Toyota Crown is something of an odd duck; priced and marketed like a premium alternative to the Lexus ES, the Audi A6, and the Acura TLX, and built on a mainstream Toyota platform that could also be cross-shopped with a loaded Camry. It landed in Toyota's lineup as the de facto replacement for the discontinued Avalon, competing in a full-size sedan segment that keeps shrinking as more buyers move to crossovers and SUVs.


Rebooted for the 2023 model year, today’s Toyota Crown blends full-size sedan proportions with the ride height and visibility of a crossover, a look that reminds us of the old Honda Accord Crosstour and the BMW 5-Series Gran Turismo. Every Crown is now a hybrid, designed to deliver Lexus-level quality and comfort for Toyota money for buyers who want a quiet, comfortable daily driver without paying for a luxury badge.


Toyota introduced the Crown name in 1955, where it soon became the brand's premium sedan—arguably the Lexus of its day. The first four generations were sold in the United States from 1958 through 1973. None of these early Toyota Crowns are meaningfully represented in the used market and have become collector cars thanks to rarity and limited sales when new.


The original Crown was engineered for Japanese roads, and struggled on American highways. Toyota fitted a larger engine to compensate, then pulled the Crown from the U.S. lineup in 1960 to focus on the Land Cruiser. The second generation returned in 1962 with more contemporary, American-influenced styling, in sedan or station wagon form.


The third generation followed in 1967 with a new frame and a more powerful inline six-cylinder engine. Toyota sold the fourth generation from 1972 to 1973, the last Crown offered in the U.S. before the Corona replaced it here, but the Crown lived on in Japan.


Thanks to the 25-year import rule, right-hand-drive Japanese-market Crowns from the 1980s and 1990s are starting to **[pop up on CarGurus](https://www.cargurus.com/Cars/l-Used-Toyota-Crown-d1156)** . Because those cars were never officially sold in the U.S., this guide doesn't cover them.

## Toyota Crown Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy

## Frequently Asked Questions


**Which Toyota Crown years are the best?**
There is no clear best model year. As a premium Toyota product, all available model years are quite reliable and easy to own. The 2025 model year featured some meaningful quality updates, from additional sound deadening to improved interior materials. At the time of writing, the 2027 model year promises to further improve the Crown with an updated hybrid system.


**Which Toyota Crown years are the worst?**
As with the best, there is no clear worst model year. The latest Toyota Crown is built on a proven platform, using a well-known hybrid system. There are some recalls to watch out for on earlier 2023 to 2025 model years, but they don't affect the overall reliability. User reports are positive, and the Crown holds up to Toyota’s well known reputation for reliability.


**Is a used Toyota Crown a good deal?**
Yes, the Toyota Crown can be a great deal. It's easy to own, reliable, and has low operating costs. Sales have been relatively low, due to its obscure position as a “crossover” luxury sedan, and that low demand continues into the used market, which means deals can be found. Even the base XLE trim is well equipped, so stepping up to the Limited or Platinum isn’t required for a luxurious experience.

## Toyota Crown Generations


## Toyota Crown First Generation (2023-Present)


The latest, 16th-generation Crown marked the nameplate's return to the U.S. after roughly 50 years, launching for the 2023 model year as a direct replacement for the Avalon. It shares a platform with other Toyota hybrids and pairs sedan proportions with a taller ride height, perfect for buyers who want the driving feel of a car with an SUV's sightlines and easy entry and exit. Every Crown is a hybrid, and every Crown comes standard with all-wheel drive.


Two hybrid powertrains are available, and both pair with Toyota’s electric all-wheel drive system. The XLE and Limited trims use the standard hybrid system—a naturally aspirated 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine paired with three electric motors, rated at a combined 236 horsepower and an EPA-estimated 41 mpg combined. Toyota launched the Crown with its fourth-generation hybrid architecture rather than the newer, more efficient fifth-generation system used elsewhere in the lineup, favoring the older version's proven track record, but it confirmed that the XLE, Limited and Nightshade will move to the fifth-generation hybrid system for the 2027 model year.


The range-topping Platinum trim uses Toyota's HybridMAX system, which pairs a turbocharged 2.4-liter four-cylinder engine and a six-speed automatic transmission with a two-motor hybrid setup tuned for performance. Total output is 340 horsepower, for a 0–60 mph time of just under six seconds, which is genuinely quick for the segment. Fuel economy suffers as a result, though, and the Platinum is rated at 30 mpg combined versus 41 mpg for the standard hybrid.


Both powertrains send power to the rear wheels through a dedicated electric motor rather than a mechanical link to the front axle. Toyota calls this Electronic On-Demand All-Wheel Drive on the XLE, Limited and Nightshade, and Full-Time Electronic All-Wheel Drive on the Platinum. It's not built for off-roading, but trades that capability for better fuel economy. On the XLE, Limited and Nightshade, the rear motor engages only as needed, while the Platinum's HybridMAX system runs full-time all-wheel drive.


The Crown lineup was launched in XLE, Limited and Platinum trims, with a Nightshade trim added for the 2025 model year. The XLE and Limited share the standard hybrid powertrain; the Platinum alone gets the more powerful HybridMAX system, an adaptive suspension that automatically adjusts for road conditions, and unique, 10-spoke 21-inch wheels. Buyers who want performance should focus on the Platinum, while those who want value or fuel economy are better served by the Limited, which adds leather upholstery, ventilated front seats, a JBL sound system and a panoramic moonroof over the base XLE, without the Platinum's fuel-economy penalty.


All Crown trims are well equipped, with eight-way power front seats and heated front and rear seats standard across the board. For 2023 and 2024, only the XLE used Toyota's SofTex synthetic leather rather than genuine leather. Starting with the 2025 model year, every trim got leather upholstery and more soft-touch materials throughout the cabin.


Every Crown uses Toyota's latest multimedia system, with a 12.3-inch touchscreen, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, and over-the-air updates through Toyota's Connected Services. The XLE gets a six-speaker audio system; the Limited, Nightshade and Platinum all get an 11-speaker JBL system. Charging ports are plentiful throughout the cabin: USB-C ports and a wireless phone charger up front, and USB-C ports in the rear. The Limited, Nightshade and Platinum also add a panoramic moonroof. Toyota insulated the cabin well, and the Crown stays notably quiet at highway speeds for the class.


Every Crown comes standard with Toyota Safety Sense 3.0, the brand's suite of driver-assistance features. It includes pre-collision braking with pedestrian detection, full-speed adaptive cruise control, a lane-departure warning with steering assist, lane-centering assist, high-beam assist and traffic-sign recognition. The Platinum adds a surround-view camera system, called Panoramic View Monitor, and that same feature is optional on the Limited as part of an Advanced Tech Package. Limited and Platinum trims also get a smart key that works on all four doors rather than just the fronts.


The 2023 Toyota Crown earned the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety's Top Safety Pick+ award, its highest honor, with Good ratings across every crashworthiness test and a superior-rated front crash prevention system.


The most significant issue on the used market is a 2024 recall filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), covering roughly 13,000 model-year 2023 Crowns built at Toyota's Motomachi plant between February and August 2023. Insufficient welding on the front and rear camera housings could allow water to seep in and short-circuit the cameras, cutting out the image. The fix is a free dealer inspection and camera replacement where needed; shoppers considering a 2023 model should confirm with the seller or a VIN check that the recall has been addressed. A broader October 2025 recall covering several Toyota models—including certain 2023-2025 Crowns—addressed a software glitch that could freeze or blank the backup camera image while reversing.


Beyond the recalls, complaints have been light. CarComplaints.com, which tracks complaints filed with NHTSA, lists only a handful across the 2023-2025 model years, a favorable sign this early in the car's life, though it's still a small sample from which to draw. Consumer Reports' subscriber survey data goes further, predicting the Crown will be more reliable than the average new car.


According to **[CarGurus pricing data](https://www.cargurus.com/research/price-trends/Toyota-Crown-d1156)** , the Toyota Crown's average price was around $37,700 at the time of writing. By model year, 2023 Crowns average roughly $33,800 with higher mileage examples starting around $25,000, while 2024 models average around $36,800, and 2025 models about $41,300. Shoppers focused on value should look at 2023-2024 Limited trims, which pair the smarter leather interior and JBL audio system with the more efficient hybrid powertrain.
